questions.question: Consider the dissociation equilibrium of the following weak acid $HA \rightleftharpoons H^{+}(aq) + A^{-}(aq)$. If the $pKa$ of the acid is 4, then the $pH$ of $10 \text{ mM} HA$ solution is _______. (Nearest integer) [Given : The degree of dissociation can be neglected with respect to unity]
questions.explanation:
For a weak acid, when the degree of dissociation is negligible with respect to unity, the \(pH\) can be calculated using the formula:

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[pKa - \log c]
$$

Given:

• \(pKa = 4\)
• Concentration \(c = 10 \text{ mM} = 10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M} = 10^{-2} \text{ M}\)

Substitute the values into the formula:

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[4 - \log 10^{-2}]
$$

Since \(\log 10^{-2} = -2\):

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[4 - (-2)]
$$

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[4 + 2]
$$

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[6]
$$

$$
pH = 3
$$

The \(pH\) of the solution is 3.

questions.question: Given below are two statements : Statements (I) : Potassium hydrogen phthalate is a primary standard for standardization of sodium hydroxide solutions. Statement (II) : In this titration phenolphthalein can be used as indicator. In the light of the above statement, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

Statement I is correct but Statement II incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Potassium hydrogen phthalate is a primary standard for standardization of sodium hydroxide solution as it is economical and its concentration does not change with time. Thus, Statement I is correct.

Phenolphthalein can act as an indicator in acid-base titrations with a pH range of 8.3 to 10.1. The titration of a weak acid (potassium hydrogen phthalate) with a strong base (sodium hydroxide) has an equivalence point in the basic region, making phenolphthalein a suitable indicator. Thus, Statement II is correct.

questions.question: Arrange the following resultant mixtures in increasing order of their pH values: • A. 10 mL 0.2 M $Ca(OH)_{{2}}$ + 25 mL 0.1 M HCl • B. 10 mL 0.01 M $H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}$ + 10 mL 0.01 M $Ca(OH)_{{2}}$ • C. 10 mL 0.1 M $H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}$ + 10 mL 0.1 M KOH Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Reactants: \(Ca(OH)_{{2}}\) (strong base) and HCl (strong acid)

Moles of \(Ca(OH)_{{2}}\) = 10 mL \(\times\) 0.2 M = 2 mmol

Moles of \(OH^{{-}}\) from \(Ca(OH)_{{2}}\) = 2 \(\times\) 2 mmol = 4 mmol

Moles of HCl = 25 mL \(\times\) 0.1 M = 2.5 mmol

Moles of \(H^{{+}}\) from HCl = 2.5 mmol

$$
H_{{(\text{aq})}}^{{+}} + OH_{{(\text{aq})}}^{{-}} \to H_{{2}}O_{{(\ell)}}
$$

At t=0: \(H^{{+}}\) = 2.5 mmol, \(OH^{{-}}\) = 4 mmol

At t=\(\infty\): \(H^{{+}}\) = 0, \(OH^{{-}}\) = 4 - 2.5 = 1.5 mmol (excess \(OH^{{-}}\))

Total volume = 10 mL + 25 mL = 35 mL

$$
[OH^{{-}}] = \frac{1.5 \text{ mmol}}{35 \text{ ml}} = \frac{1.5}{35}
$$

$$
\text{pOH} = -\log \frac{1.5}{35}
$$

$$
\text{pH} = 14 + \log \left( \frac{1.5}{35} \right)
$$

Calculating the value: \(\log(1.5/35) \approx \log(0.0428) \approx -1.36\)

\(\text{pH} \approx 14 - 1.36 = 12.64\)

Reactants: \(H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}\) (strong acid) and \(Ca(OH)_{{2}}\) (strong base)

Moles of \(H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}\) = 10 mL \(\times\) 0.01 M = 0.1 mmol

Moles of \(H^{{+}}\) from \(H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}\) = 2 \(\times\) 0.1 mmol = 0.2 mmol

Moles of \(Ca(OH)_{{2}}\) = 10 mL \(\times\) 0.01 M = 0.1 mmol

Moles of \(OH^{{-}}\) from \(Ca(OH)_{{2}}\) = 2 \(\times\) 0.1 mmol = 0.2 mmol

$$
H_{{(\text{aq})}}^{{+}} + OH_{{(\text{aq})}}^{{-}} \to H_{{2}}O_{{(\ell)}}
$$

At t=0: \(H^{{+}}\) = 0.2 mmol, \(OH^{{-}}\) = 0.2 mmol

At t=\(\infty\): \(H^{{+}}\) = 0, \(OH^{{-}}\) = 0 (neutral solution)

Final pH = 7

Reactants: \(H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}\) (strong acid) and KOH (strong base)

Moles of \(H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}\) = 10 mL \(\times\) 0.1 M = 1 mmol

Moles of \(H^{{+}}\) from \(H_{{2}}SO_{{4}}\) = 2 \(\times\) 1 mmol = 2 mmol

Moles of KOH = 10 mL \(\times\) 0.1 M = 1 mmol

Moles of \(OH^{{-}}\) from KOH = 1 mmol

$$
H_{{(\text{aq})}}^{{+}} + OH_{{(\text{aq})}}^{{-}} \to H_{{2}}O_{{(\ell)}}
$$

At t=0: \(H^{{+}}\) = 2 mmol, \(OH^{{-}}\) = 1 mmol

At t=\(\infty\): \(H^{{+}}\) = 1 mmol (excess \(H^{{+}}\)), \(OH^{{-}}\) = 0

Total volume = 10 mL + 10 mL = 20 mL

$$
[H^{{+}}] = \frac{1 \text{ mmol}}{20 \text{ ml}} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05 \text{ M}
$$

$$
\text{pH} = -\log(0.05) = -\log(5 \times 10^{{-2}}) = 2 - \log(5) \approx 2 - 0.7 = 1.3
$$

\(\text{pH(A)} \approx 12.64\)

\(\text{pH(B)} = 7\)

\(\text{pH(C)} \approx 1.3\)

\(\text{pH(C)} < \text{pH(B)} < \text{pH(A)}\)

\(1.3 < 7 < 12.64\)

This corresponds to the order C < B < A.

questions.question: The solubility product constants of $Ag_{2}CrO_{4}$ and $AgBr$ are $32x$ and $4y$ respectively at $298$ K. The value of  \left(\frac{\text{molarity of } Ag_{2}CrO_{4}}{\text{molarity of } AgBr}\right)$$ can be expressed as :
questions.explanation:
For \(Ag_{2}CrO_{4}\), let its solubility be \(S_{1}\).

$$
Ag_{2}CrO_{4}(s) \rightleftharpoons 2Ag^{+}(aq) + CrO_{4}^{2-}(aq)
$$

The solubility product constant \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}\) is given by \(K_{\mathrm{sp}} = [Ag^{+}]^{2}[CrO_{4}^{2-}] = (2S_{1})^{2}(S_{1}) = 4S_{1}^{3}\).

Given \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}(Ag_{2}CrO_{4}) = 32x\).

$$
4S_{1}^{3} = 32x
$$

$$
S_{1}^{3} = 8x
$$

$$
S_{1} = (8x)^{1/3} = 2x^{1/3}
$$

For \(AgBr\), let its solubility be \(S_{2}\).

$$
AgBr(s) \rightleftharpoons Ag^{+}(aq) + Br^{-}(aq)
$$

The solubility product constant \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}\) is given by \(K_{\mathrm{sp}} = [Ag^{+}][Br^{-}] = (S_{2})(S_{2}) = S_{2}^{2}\).

Given \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}(AgBr) = 4y\).

$$
S_{2}^{2} = 4y
$$

$$
S_{2} = (4y)^{1/2} = 2y^{1/2}
$$

The ratio of molarity of \(Ag_{2}CrO_{4}\) to molarity of \(AgBr\) is \(S_{1}/S_{2}\).

$$
\frac{S_{1}}{S_{2}} = \frac{2x^{1/3}}{2y^{1/2}}
$$

$$
\frac{S_{1}}{S_{2}} = \frac{x^{1/3}}{y^{1/2}}
$$

$$
\frac{S_{1}}{S_{2}} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{x}}{\sqrt{y}}
$$

This matches option (4).

questions.question: If 1 mM solution of ethylamine produces pH = 9, then the ionization constant ($K_{b}$) of ethylamine is $10^{-x}$. The value of x is ______ (nearest integer). [The degree of ionization of ethylamine can be neglected with respect to unity.]
questions.explanation:
$$
C_{2}H_{5}NH_{2}(aq) + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons C_{2}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+} + OH^{\ominus}
$$

Given, \(pH = 9 \Rightarrow pOH = 5 \Rightarrow [OH^{\ominus}] = 10^{-5} M\)

From the equilibrium concentrations, we have \([OH^{\ominus}] = C\alpha = 10^{-5}\) and \([C_{2}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+}] = C\alpha = 10^{-5}\).

Since the degree of ionization \(\alpha\) can be neglected with respect to unity, \(1 - \alpha \approx 1\).

$$
\text{Now, } K_{b} = \frac{[C_{2}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+}][OH^{\ominus}]}{[C_{2}H_{5}NH_{2}]}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow K_{b} = \frac{10^{-5} \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-3}} = 10^{-7}
$$

Comparing this with \(K_{b} = 10^{-x}\), we get \(x = 7\).

questions.question: Ksp for $Cr(OH)_{3}$ is $1.6 \times 10^{-30}$. What is the molar solubility of this salt in water?
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The dissociation of \(Cr(OH)_{3}\) in water is given by:

$$
Cr(OH)_{3 \text{(s)}} \rightleftharpoons Cr^{3+}_{\text{(aq)}} + 3OH^{-}_{\text{(aq)}}
$$

At equilibrium, if 's' is the molar solubility of \(Cr(OH)_{3}\), then the concentrations of ions are:

\([Cr^{3+}] = s\)

\([OH^{-}] = 3s\)

The solubility product constant \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}\) is given by:

$$
K_{\mathrm{sp}} = [Cr^{3+}][OH^{-}]^3
$$

Substitute the equilibrium concentrations:

$$
K_{\mathrm{sp}} = (s)(3s)^3 = s \cdot 27s^3 = 27s^4
$$

Given \(K_{\mathrm{sp}} = 1.6 \times 10^{-30}\):

$$
27s^4 = 1.6 \times 10^{-30}
$$

Solve for 's':

$$
s^4 = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-30}}{27}
$$

$$
s = \left(\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-30}}{27}\right)^{1/4}
$$

$$
s = \sqrt[4]{\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-30}}{27}}
$$

This matches option (1).

questions.question: 20 mL of 0.1 M NaOH is added to 50 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid solution. The pH of the resulting solution is ________ $\times 10^{-2}$ (Nearest integer) Given : $$$\mathrm{pKa} \left$($\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH} \right$)$ = 4.76 \log 2 = 0.30 \log 3 = 0.48$
questions.explanation:
The reaction is between acetic acid (a weak acid) and sodium hydroxide (a strong base):

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COONa} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}
$$

Initial moles of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) = Volume \(\times\) Concentration = \(50 \text{ mL} \times 0.1 \text{ M} = 5 \text{ mmol}\)

Initial moles of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) = Volume \(\times\) Concentration = \(20 \text{ mL} \times 0.1 \text{ M} = 2 \text{ mmol}\)

Since \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is the limiting reactant, it will be completely consumed. The reaction consumes 2 mmol of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) and produces 2 mmol of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COONa}\).

After the reaction, we have a buffer solution containing \(3 \text{ mmol}\) of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) (weak acid) and \(2 \text{ mmol}\) of \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COONa}\) (conjugate base).

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer is:

$$
\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{pKa} + \log_{10} \frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}
$$

Substitute the given \(\mathrm{pKa}\) value and the moles of salt and acid (concentrations can be used directly as the total volume is the same for both):

$$
\mathrm{pH} = 4.76 + \log_{10} \frac{2 \text{ mmol}}{3 \text{ mmol}}
$$

$$
\mathrm{pH} = 4.76 + \log_{10} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)
$$

Using logarithm properties, \(\log_{10} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = \log_{10} 2 - \log_{10} 3\)

Given \(\log 2 = 0.30\) and \(\log 3 = 0.48\).

$$
\mathrm{pH} = 4.76 + (0.30 - 0.48)
$$

$$
\mathrm{pH} = 4.76 - 0.18
$$

$$
\mathrm{pH} = 4.58
$$

The question asks for the pH in the format \( \_ \times 10^{-2}\) (Nearest integer).

$$
\mathrm{pH} = 4.58 = 458 \times 10^{-2}
$$

The nearest integer to fill the blank is 458.

questions.question: A litre of buffer solution contains 0.1 mole of each of $NH_{3}$ and $NH_{4}Cl$. On the addition of 0.02 mole of $HCl$ by dissolving gaseous $HCl$, the $pH$ of the solution is found to be $\underline{\hspace{1cm}} \times 10^{-3}$ (Nearest integer) [Given : $pK_{b}(NH_{3}) = 4.745$, $\log 2 = 0.301$, $\log 3 = 0.477$, $T = 298 K$]
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Initial moles of \(NH_{3}\) and \(NH_{4}Cl\) are 0.1 mole each. 0.02 mole of \(HCl\) is added. The reaction is as follows:

$$
NH_{3} + HCl \rightarrow NH_{4}Cl
$$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer:

$$
pOH = pK_{b} + \log \frac{[NH_{4}Cl]}{[NH_{3}]}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pOH = 4.745 + \log \left(\frac{0.12}{0.08}\right)
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pOH = 4.745 + \log \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pOH = 4.745 + (\log 3 - \log 2)
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pOH = 4.745 + (0.477 - 0.301)
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pOH = 4.745 + 0.176
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pOH = 4.569
$$

Since \(pH + pOH = 14\):

$$
pH = 14 - pOH
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pH = 14 - 4.569
$$

$$
\Rightarrow pH = 9.431
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer:

$$
\Rightarrow pH \approx 9
$$

questions.question: Given below are two statement : Statement I : In redox titration, the indicators used are sensitive to change in pH of the solution. Statement II : In acid-base titration, the indicators used are sensitive to change in oxidation potential. In the light of the above statement, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
questions.explanation:
Statement I says: "In redox titration, the indicators used are sensitive to change in pH of the solution."

Redox titrations involve a change in the oxidation state of the reactants, and thus the indicators used in redox titrations are sensitive to changes in the oxidation potential (or electrode potential) of the solution, not pH. pH indicators are used for acid-base titrations. Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.

Statement II says: "In acid-base titration, the indicators used are sensitive to change in oxidation potential."

Acid-base titrations involve a change in the concentration of \(H^{+}\) or \(OH^{-}\) ions, leading to a change in the pH of the solution. The indicators used in acid-base titrations are sensitive to changes in pH. Indicators sensitive to oxidation potential are used in redox titrations. Therefore, Statement II is incorrect.

Since both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect, the most appropriate answer is the option that states both are incorrect.

questions.question: The pH of a 0.01 M weak acid HX ($K_{a} = 4 \times 10^{-10}$) is found to be 5. Now the acid solution is diluted with excess of water so that the pH of the solution changes to 6. The new concentration of the diluted weak acid is given as $x \times 10^{-4}$ M. The value of x is ____ (nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given initial concentration \(C_{1} = 0.01\) M and initial \(pH_{1} = 5\).

From \(pH_{1} = 5\), we have \([H^{+}]_{1} = 10^{-5}\) M.

For a weak acid \(HX_{(aq)} \rightleftharpoons H^{+}_{(aq)} + X^{-}_{(aq)}\), the acid dissociation constant \(K_{a}\) is given by:

$$
K_{a} = \frac{[H^{+}][X^{-}]}{[HX]} = \frac{[H^{+}]^{2}}{C_{1} - [H^{+}]}
$$

Substituting the initial values:

$$
K_{a} = \frac{(10^{-5})^{2}}{0.01 - 10^{-5}} = \frac{10^{-10}}{0.00999} \approx 10^{-8}
$$

This calculated \(K_{a}\) (approximately \(10^{-8}\)) contradicts the \(K_{a}\) value given in the problem (\(K_{a} = 4 \times 10^{-10}\)). This indicates an inconsistency in the problem statement.

To arrive at the NTA answer, we proceed by assuming the given \(K_{a} = 4 \times 10^{-10}\) is correct and use the final \(pH_{2} = 6\) to determine the new concentration.

From \(pH_{2} = 6\), we have \([H^{+}]_{2} = 10^{-6}\) M.

Let the new concentration of the diluted weak acid be \(C_{2}\).

For the weak acid equilibrium, \(K_{a} = \frac{[H^{+}][X^{-}]}{[HX]}\). Since \([H^{+}] = [X^{-}]\) and \([HX] \approx C_{2} - [H^{+}]\).

Given that \(K_{a}\) is very small (\(4 \times 10^{-10}\)) and \([H^{+}] = 10^{-6}\) M, the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) will be small. Thus, we can approximate \([HX] \approx C_{2}\) (i.e., \(C_{2} \gg [H^{+}]\)).

So, the expression for \(K_{a}\) simplifies to:

$$
K_{a} \approx \frac{[H^{+}]^{2}}{C_{2}}
$$

Substituting the values:

$$
4 \times 10^{-10} = \frac{(10^{-6})^{2}}{C_{2}}
$$

$$
4 \times 10^{-10} = \frac{10^{-12}}{C_{2}}
$$

$$
C_{2} = \frac{10^{-12}}{4 \times 10^{-10}} = \frac{1}{4} \times 10^{-2}
$$

$$
C_{2} = 0.25 \times 10^{-2} = 25 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}
$$

The new concentration is given as \(x \times 10^{-4}\) M.

Comparing this with our calculated \(C_{2}\):

$$
x \times 10^{-4} = 25 \times 10^{-4}
$$

$$
x = 25
$$

The value of x is 25 (nearest integer).

As noted in the original solution: Data given is inconsistent & contradictory. This should be bonus.

questions.question: For a concentrated solution of a weak electrolyte ($K_{\mathrm{eq}}$ = equilibrium constant) $A_2B_3$ of concentration 'c', the degree of dissociation "$\alpha$" is
questions.explanation:
$$
A_2B_3(\mathrm{aq.}) \rightleftharpoons 2A^{3+}_{(\mathrm{aq.})} + 3B^{2-}_{(\mathrm{aq.})}
$$

Initial concentration:

$$
c \quad 0 \quad 0
$$

At equilibrium (assuming \(\alpha\) is small for concentrated solution, but the problem doesn't explicitly state to approximate \(1-\alpha \approx 1\), so we keep \(1-\alpha\) for now, though the solution simplifies it later):

$$
c(1-\alpha) \quad 2c\alpha \quad 3c\alpha
$$

$$
K_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{[A^{3+}]^2 [B^{2-}]^3}{[A_2B_3]}
$$

$$
K_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{(2c\alpha)^2 (3c\alpha)^3}{c(1-\alpha)}
$$

$$
K_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{(4c^2\alpha^2) (27c^3\alpha^3)}{c(1-\alpha)}
$$

$$
K_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{108c^5\alpha^5}{c(1-\alpha)}
$$

For a concentrated solution of a weak electrolyte, the degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) is generally very small, so \(1-\alpha \approx 1\). (This approximation is implicitly used in the provided solution to get the final form).

$$
K_{\mathrm{eq}} \approx \frac{108c^5\alpha^5}{c}
$$

$$
K_{\mathrm{eq}} = 108c^4\alpha^5
$$

$$
\alpha^5 = \frac{K_{\mathrm{eq}}}{108c^4}
$$

$$
\alpha = \left(\frac{K_{\mathrm{eq}}}{108c^4}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}
$$

questions.question: At 298 K, the solubility of silver chloride in water is $1.434 \times 10^{-3}$ g $L^{-1}$. The value of $-\log K_{sp}$ for silver chloride is (Given mass of Ag is 107.9 g $mol^{-1}$ and mass of Cl is 35.5 g $mol^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation:
Given solubility of AgCl (S) = \(1.434 \times 10^{-3}\) g/L

Molar mass of Ag = 107.9 g/mol

Molar mass of Cl = 35.5 g/mol

Molar mass of AgCl = Mass of Ag + Mass of Cl = \(107.9 + 35.5 = 143.4\) g/mol

To find the solubility in mol/L (M), divide the solubility in g/L by the molar mass of AgCl:

$$
S = \frac{1.434 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g/L}}{143.4 \text{ g/mol}}
$$

$$
S = 10^{-5} \text{ mol/L}
$$

Silver chloride (AgCl) is a sparingly soluble salt. Its dissolution equilibrium in water is:

$$
\text{AgCl(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})
$$

If S is the molar solubility of AgCl, then \([\text{Ag}^+] = S\) and \([\text{Cl}^-] = S\).

The solubility product constant \(K_{sp}\) is given by:

$$
K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Cl}^-] = S \times S = S^2
$$

Substitute the calculated molar solubility (S) into the \(K_{sp}\) expression:

$$
K_{sp} = (10^{-5})^2 = 10^{-10}
$$

The problem asks for the value of \(-\log K_{sp}\):

$$
-\log K_{sp} = -\log(10^{-10})
$$

$$
-\log K_{sp} = -(-10)
$$

$$
-\log K_{sp} = 10
$$

questions.question: Only litre buffer solution was prepared by adding 0.10 mol each of $NH_{3}$ and $NH_{4}Cl$ in deionised water. The change in pH on addition of 0.05 mol of $HCl$ to the above solution is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}\ \times 10^{-2}$, (Nearest integer) (Given : $pK_{b}$ of $NH_{3} = 4.745$ and $\log_{10}3 = 0.477$)
questions.explanation:
Initially, we have a buffer solution containing \(NH_{3}\) (weak base) and \(NH_{4}Cl\) (salt of weak base and strong acid, providing \(NH_{4}^{+}\)).

Given that 0.10 mol each of \(NH_{3}\) and \(NH_{4}Cl\) are added to 1 litre of deionised water, the initial concentrations are:

$$
[NH_{3}] = 0.10\ M
$$

$$
[NH_{4}^{+}] = 0.10\ M
$$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer:

$$
pOH = pK_{b} + \log \frac{[NH_{4}^{+}]}{[NH_{3}]}
$$

Substitute the given values:

$$
pOH = 4.745 + \log \frac{0.10}{0.10} = 4.745 + \log 1 = 4.745
$$

Now, 0.05 mol of \(HCl\) (a strong acid) is added to the buffer solution. \(HCl\) will react with the weak base \(NH_{3}\):

$$
NH_{3} + H^{\oplus} \rightarrow NH_{4}^{\oplus}
$$

Initial moles:

$$
NH_{3}: 0.10\ mol
$$

$$
H^{\oplus}: 0.05\ mol
$$

$$
NH_{4}^{\oplus}: 0.10\ mol
$$

After reaction (0.05 mol of \(NH_{3}\) reacts with 0.05 mol of \(H^{\oplus}\)):

$$
NH_{3}: 0.10 - 0.05 = 0.05\ mol
$$

$$
H^{\oplus}: 0.05 - 0.05 = 0\ mol
$$

$$
NH_{4}^{\oplus}: 0.10 + 0.05 = 0.15\ mol
$$

Since the total volume is 1 litre, the new concentrations are:

$$
[NH_{3}]' = 0.05\ M
$$

$$
[NH_{4}^{+}]' = 0.15\ M
$$

Calculate the new pOH (pOH'):

$$
pOH' = pK_{b} + \log \frac{[NH_{4}^{+}]'}{[NH_{3}]'}
$$

$$
pOH' = 4.745 + \log \frac{0.15}{0.05} = 4.745 + \log 3
$$

Given \(\log_{10}3 = 0.477\):

$$
pOH' = 4.745 + 0.477 = 5.222
$$

The change in pOH is:

$$
\Delta pOH = pOH' - pOH = 5.222 - 4.745 = 0.477
$$

We know that \(pH + pOH = 14\). Therefore, a change in pOH corresponds to an opposite change in pH:

$$
\Delta pH = pH' - pH = (14 - pOH') - (14 - pOH) = pOH - pOH' = -\Delta pOH
$$

$$
\Delta pH = -0.477
$$

The question asks for the magnitude of the change in pH, so we take the absolute value:

$$
|\Delta pH| = |-0.477| = 0.477
$$

We need to express this value as \(\underline{\hspace{1cm}}\ \times 10^{-2}\). So, we convert 0.477:

$$
0.477 = 47.7 \times 10^{-2}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the value is 48.

$$
|\Delta pH| \approx 48 \times 10^{-2}
$$

20 mL of a solution of acetic acid required 28.4 mL of 0.1 M NaOH for its neutralization. A solution (X) was prepared by mixing 20 mL of the above acetic acid and 14.2 mL of 0.1 M NaOH solution. What is the pH of the solution (X) ? ($pK_{a}$ value of acetic acid is 4.75).
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

First, we use the information from the complete neutralization to find the initial amount of acetic acid. The reaction is:

$$
CH_{3}COOH + NaOH \to CH_{3}COONa + H_{2}O
$$

The moles of NaOH required for complete neutralization are calculated as:

$$
\text{Moles of NaOH} = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume} = 0.1 \, \text{M} \times 0.0284 \, \text{L} = 0.00284 \, \text{mol}
$$

At the equivalence point, the moles of acetic acid are equal to the moles of NaOH. Therefore, the 20 mL solution of acetic acid contains 0.00284 moles of \(CH_{3}COOH\).

Solution (X) is prepared by mixing 20 mL of this acetic acid solution with 14.2 mL of 0.1 M NaOH. The moles of NaOH added are:

$$
\text{Moles of NaOH added} = 0.1 \, \text{M} \times 0.0142 \, \text{L} = 0.00142 \, \text{mol}
$$

When NaOH reacts with acetic acid:

• Moles of \(CH_{3}COONa\) (salt) formed = Moles of NaOH added = 0.00142 mol.
• Moles of \(CH_{3}COOH\) (acid) remaining = Initial moles - Moles reacted = 0.00284 - 0.00142 = 0.00142 mol.

The resulting solution contains equal moles of a weak acid (\(CH_{3}COOH\)) and its conjugate base (\(CH_{3}COONa\)). This is a buffer solution. The point where exactly half of the acid has been neutralized (14.2 mL of NaOH is half of 28.4 mL) is known as the half-equivalence point.

We use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation to find the pH:

$$
pH = pK_{a} + \log\left(\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\right)
$$

At the half-equivalence point, the concentration of the salt is equal to the concentration of the remaining acid, because their mole amounts are equal and they are in the same total volume.

$$
[\text{Salt}] = [\text{Acid}]
$$

Therefore, the ratio \(\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\) is 1, and \(\log(1) = 0\).

$$
pH = pK_{a} + \log(1) = pK_{a} + 0
$$

$$
pH = pK_{a}
$$

Given that the \(pK_{a}\) of acetic acid is 4.75, the pH of the solution is:

$$
pH = 4.75
$$

Note: Based on the provided data, the calculated pH is 4.75. However, the provided answer key indicates option (2) 4.45, which suggests a possible typo in the question's pKₐ value or the options.

items.text: $x_{3} BaSO_{4}$ is sparingly soluble in water. If the conductivity of the saturated $BaSO_{4}$ solution is x S cm⁻¹ then the solubility product of $BaSO_{4}$ can be given as.

questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For a sparingly soluble salt like \(BaSO_{4}\), the dissociation equilibrium is:

$$
BaSO_{4}(s) \rightleftharpoons Ba_{(aq)}^{+2} + SO_{4(aq)}^{2-}
$$

If 'S' is the molar solubility, then at equilibrium, \([Ba^{2+}] = S\) and \([SO_{4}^{2-}] = S\). The solubility product, \(K_{sp}\), is given by:

$$
K_{sp} = [Ba^{2+}][SO_{4}^{2-}] = S \times S = S^{2}
$$

The conductivity (specific conductance), k, of the saturated solution is given as x S cm⁻¹.

$$
k = x \text{ S cm}^{-1}
$$

The molar conductivity at infinite dilution, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\), for \(BaSO_{4}\) can be calculated using Kohlrausch's law from the given data:

$$
\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4}) = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaCl_{2}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(H_{2}SO_{4}) - 2 \times \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(HCl)
$$

$$
\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4}) = x_{1} + x_{2} - 2x_{3}
$$

The relationship between molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{m}\)), specific conductivity (k), and molar solubility (S) is:

$$
\Lambda_{m} = \frac{k \times 1000}{S}
$$

Also, the molar conductivity is related to the molar conductivity at infinite dilution and the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) by:

$$
\Lambda_{m} = \alpha \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}
$$

Equating the two expressions for \(\Lambda_{m}\):

$$
\alpha \Lambda_{m}^{\circ} = \frac{k \times 1000}{S}
$$

Now, we can solve for the solubility S:

$$
S = \frac{k \times 1000}{\alpha \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}
$$

Substituting the given values:

$$
S = \frac{x \times 1000}{\alpha (x_{1} + x_{2} - 2x_{3})}
$$

Finally, we calculate the solubility product, \(K_{sp}\):

$$
K_{sp} = S^{2} = \left( \frac{x \times 1000}{\alpha (x_{1} + x_{2} - 2x_{3})} \right)^{2}
$$

$$
K_{sp} = \frac{x^{2} \times (1000)^{2}}{\alpha^{2} (x_{1} + x_{2} - 2x_{3})^{2}} = \frac{10^{6} x^{2}}{\alpha^{2}(x_{1} + x_{2} - 2x_{3})^{2}}
$$

questions.question: Incorrect statement for the use of indicators in acid-base titration is :
options: Methyl orange may be used for a weak acid vs weak base titration.
Phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for a weak acid vs strong base titration.
Methyl orange is a suitable indicator for a strong acid vs weak base titration.
Phenolphthalein may be used for a strong acid vs strong base titration.
questions.explanation:
For a weak acid – weak base titration, the pH change at the equivalence point is very small and gradual. Therefore, neither phenolphthalein nor methyl orange (or any common indicator) is suitable for such a titration.

Let's review the suitability of indicators for different titrations:

• Strong acid vs Strong base: Equivalence point at pH 7. Both methyl orange (pH range 3.1-4.4) and phenolphthalein (pH range 8.2-10) are suitable as the pH changes sharply over a wide range.
• Weak acid vs Strong base: Equivalence point at pH > 7 (basic). Phenolphthalein is suitable.
• Strong acid vs Weak base: Equivalence point at pH < 7 (acidic). Methyl orange is suitable.
• Weak acid vs Weak base: No suitable indicator due to a very small and gradual pH change at the equivalence point.

Based on this, the statement that 'Methyl orange may be used for a weak acid vs weak base titration' is incorrect.

We have three aqueous solutions of NaCl labelled as 'A', 'B' and 'C' with concentration 0.1 M, 0.01 M and 0.001 M, respectively. The value of van 't Hoff factor($i$) for these solutions will be in the order :
questions.explanation:
According to Ostwald's law of Dilution, as dilution increases (i.e., concentration decreases), the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) of an electrolyte increases. The van 't Hoff factor (\(i\)) is related to the degree of dissociation by the formula \(i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha\), where \(n\) is the number of ions produced per formula unit (for NaCl, \(n=2\)).

Given concentrations:

• Solution A: 0.1 M
• Solution B: 0.01 M
• Solution C: 0.001 M

The order of concentration is \(C_{A} \gt C_{B} \gt C_{C}\). Therefore, the order of dilution is \(D_{A} \lt D_{B} \lt D_{C}\).

Since the degree of dissociation increases with dilution, we have \(\alpha_{A} \lt \alpha_{B} \lt \alpha_{C}\).

As \(i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha\) and \(n=2\) for NaCl, \(i = 1 + \alpha\). Since \(i\) is directly proportional to \(\alpha\), the order of van 't Hoff factors will be the same as the order of dissociation.

Thus, \(i_{A} \lt i_{B} \lt i_{C}\).

$$

$$

$$
\text{Molarity of acid} = \frac{1.21 \times 10^3 \text{ g/L}}{24.2 \text{ g/mol}} = \frac{1210}{24.2} = 50 \text{ M}
$$

The neutralization reaction for a monobasic strong acid (HA) and NaOH is:

$$
\text{HA} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaA} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}
$$

For complete neutralization, the moles of acid must equal the moles of base. Using the formula \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) (where 1 is for acid and 2 is for base):

$$
M_{\text{acid}} V_{\text{acid}} = M_{\text{NaOH}} V_{\text{NaOH}}
$$

$$
50 \text{ M} \times V_{\text{acid}} = 0.24 \text{ M} \times 25 \text{ mL}
$$

$$
V_{\text{acid}} = \frac{0.24 \times 25}{50} \text{ mL}
$$

$$
V_{\text{acid}} = \frac{6}{50} \text{ mL} = 0.12 \text{ mL}
$$

The problem asks for the volume in the format \(X \times 10^{-2}\) mL (Nearest integer).

$$
0.12 \text{ mL} = X \times 10^{-2} \text{ mL}
$$

$$
X = \frac{0.12}{10^{-2}} = 0.12 \times 100 = 12
$$

The nearest integer is 12.

questions.question: Given is a concentrated solution of a weak electrolyte $A_{x}B_{y}$ of concentration 'c' and dissociation constant 'K'. the degree of dissociation is given by: [K \times $c^{x+y-1} x^x y^y$]^{x+y}
questions.explanation:
Let the weak electrolyte be \(A_{x}B_{y}\). Its dissociation can be represented as:

$$
A_{x}B_{y} \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}
$$

Initial concentration:

$$
C \quad \quad \quad 0 \quad \quad 0
$$

At equilibrium (with degree of dissociation \(\alpha\)):

$$
C(1 - \alpha) \quad xC\alpha \quad yC\alpha
$$

The dissociation constant \(K\) is given by:

$$
K = \frac{[A^{y+}]^x [B^{x-}]^y}{[A_x B_y]} = \frac{(xC\alpha)^x (yC\alpha)^y}{C(1 - \alpha)}
$$

Simplifying the expression:

$$
K = \frac{x^x C^x \alpha^x y^y C^y \alpha^y}{C(1 - \alpha)} = \frac{x^x y^y C^{x+y} \alpha^{x+y}}{C(1 - \alpha)}
$$

$$
K = \frac{x^x y^y C^{x+y-1} \alpha^{x+y}}{(1 - \alpha)}
$$

For a weak electrolyte, the degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) is very small, so we can approximate \((1 - \alpha) \approx 1\).

$$
K = x^x y^y C^{x+y-1} \alpha^{x+y}
$$

Now, we solve for \(\alpha\):

$$
\alpha^{x+y} = \frac{K}{x^x y^y C^{x+y-1}}
$$

$$
\alpha = \left(\frac{K}{x^x y^y C^{x+y-1}}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}}
$$

Comparing this with the given options, option (2) matches our derived expression.

questions.question: Solubility of calcium phosphate (molecular mass, M) in water is $W_g$ per $100$ mL at $25^{\circ}C$. Its solubility product at $25^{\circ}C$ will be approximately.
questions.explanation:
At \(25^{\circ}C\), the dissociation of calcium phosphate is:

$$
Ca_{3}(PO_{4})_{2} \rightarrow 3 Ca^{+2} + 2 PO_{4}^{-3}
$$

If \(S\) is the molar solubility, then the concentrations of the ions are \([Ca^{+2}] = 3S\) and \([PO_{4}^{-3}] = 2S\).

$$
K_{SP} = [Ca^{+2}]^3 [PO_{4}^{-3}]^2
$$

$$
= (3S)^3 (2S)^2
$$

Given that solubility is \(W_g\) per \(100\) mL, and molecular mass is \(M\). So, \(S = \frac{W}{M}\) mol per \(100\) mL.

The concentrations in \(100\) mL are \(\left[\frac{3W}{M}\right]\) and \(\left[\frac{2W}{M}\right]\). Since molarity is measured in litre, we convert the concentrations by multiplying by \(\frac{1000}{100} = 10\):

$$
K_{SP} = \left[\frac{3W}{M} \times 10\right]^3 \left[\frac{2W}{M} \times 10\right]^2
$$

$$
= \left[\frac{30W}{M}\right]^3 \left[\frac{20W}{M}\right]^2
$$

$$
= (30)^3 \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^3 \times (20)^2 \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^2
$$

$$
= (27000 \times 400) \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^{3+2}
$$

$$
= 10800000 \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^5
$$

$$
= 108 \times 10^5 \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^5
$$

Approximating \(108 \approx 10^2\):

$$
K_{SP} \approx 10^2 \times 10^5 \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^5
$$

$$
K_{SP} \approx 10^7 \left(\frac{W}{M}\right)^5
$$

H\(_{2}\)SO\(_{4}\) is a strong acid and provides 2 H\(^{+}\) ions per molecule. Moles of H\(^{+}\) from H\(_{2}\)SO\(_{4}\) = 2 \(\times\) Molarity \(\times\) Volume = \(2 \times 0.01 \times 400 = 8\) millimoles.

Total volume of the mixture = 600 mL + 400 mL = 1000 mL.

The concentration of H\(^{+}\) in the mixture is:

$$
[H^{+}]_{mix} = \frac{\text{Total millimoles of } H^{+}}{\text{Total volume in mL}} = \frac{(600 \times 0.01) + (400 \times 0.01 \times 2)}{1000}
$$

$$
= \frac{6+8}{1000} = \frac{14}{1000} = 14 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M}
$$

Now, calculate the pH:

$$
pH = -\log[H^{+}] = -\log(14 \times 10^{-3})
$$

$$
pH = -(\log 14 + \log 10^{-3}) = 3 - \log 14
$$

$$
pH = 3 - \log(2 \times 7) = 3 - (\log 2 + \log 7)
$$

Using the given values:

$$
pH = 3 - 0.30 - 0.84 = 3 - 1.14 = 1.86

The question asks for the pH in the form \(x \times 10^{-2}\). Therefore:

questions.question: The first and second ionization constants of a weak dibasic acid $H_{2}A$ are $8.1 \times 10^{-8}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-13}$ respectively. $0.1$ mol of $H_{2}A$ was dissolved in $1L$ of $0.1 M HCl$ solution. The concentration of $HA^{-}$ in the resultant solution is :
questions.explanation:
Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a strong acid and dissociates completely:

$$
HCl \to H^{+} + Cl^{-}
$$

Initial concentrations:

$$
\text{0.1 M} \quad \text{0} \quad \text{0}
$$

After dissociation:

$$
\text{0} \quad \text{0.1 M} \quad \text{0.1 M}
$$

So, the concentration of \(H^{+}\) ions from \(HCl\) is \([H^{+}]_{\text{HCl}} = 0.1\) \(M\).

The first dissociation of the weak acid \(H_{2}A\) is:

$$
H_{2}A \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + HA^{-}
$$

Let \(x\) be the concentration of \(HA^{-}\) formed at equilibrium. The initial concentration of \(H_{2}A\) is \(0.1\) \(M\), and the initial concentration of \(H^{+}\) from \(HCl\) is \(0.1\) \(M\).

Equilibrium concentrations:

$$
[H_{2}A] = 0.1 - x
$$

$$
[H^{+}] = 0.1 + x
$$

$$
[HA^{-}] = x
$$

Due to the common ion effect (from \(H^{+}\) supplied by \(HCl\)), the dissociation of \(H_{2}A\) will be suppressed, meaning \(x\) will be very small compared to \(0.1\). Therefore, we can make the following approximations:

$$
[H_{2}A] \approx 0.1 \text{ M}
$$

$$
[H^{+}] \approx 0.1 \text{ M}
$$

The expression for the first ionization constant \(K_{a1}\) is:

$$
K_{a1} = \frac{[H^{+}][HA^{-}]}{[H_{2}A]}
$$

Given \(K_{a1} = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}\). Substitute the approximate equilibrium concentrations:

$$
8.1 \times 10^{-8} = \frac{(0.1)(x)}{0.1}
$$

Solving for \(x\):

$$
x = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}
$$

Since \([HA^{-}] = x\), the concentration of \(HA^{-}\) in the resultant solution is \(8.1 \times 10^{-8}\) \(M\).

The pH is defined as \(pH = -\log_{10}[H^+]\).

If the hydrogen ion concentration \([H^+]\) changes by a factor of 1000, it means the new concentration \([H^+]' = 1000 \times [H^+]\).

The new pH value will be:

questions.question: $M_{3}A_{2}$ is a sparingly soluble salt of molar mass y g $mol^{-1}$ and solubility x g $L^{-1}$. The ratio of the molar concentration of the anion ($A^{-3}$) to the solubility product of the salt is
questions.explanation:
The sparingly soluble salt \(M_{3}A_{2}\) dissociates as follows:

$$
M_{3}A_{2}(s) \rightleftharpoons 3M^{+2}(aq.) + 2A^{-3}(aq.)
$$

Given solubility = x g \(L^{-1}\) and molar mass = y g \(mol^{-1}\).

Molarity of \(M_{3}A_{2}\) (s) = \(\frac{\text{solubility (g/L)}}{\text{molar mass (g/mol)}} = \frac{x}{y}\) mol \(L^{-1}\).

From the stoichiometry of the dissociation:

$$
[M^{+2}] = 3 \times \frac{x}{y} = \frac{3x}{y}
$$

$$
[A^{-3}] = 2 \times \frac{x}{y} = \frac{2x}{y}
$$

The solubility product expression for \(M_{3}A_{2}\) is:

$$
K_{sp} = [M^{+2}]^3 [A^{-3}]^2
$$

Substitute the equilibrium concentrations:

$$
K_{sp} = \left[\frac{3x}{y}\right]^3 \left[\frac{2x}{y}\right]^2
$$

$$
K_{sp} = \left(\frac{27x^3}{y^3}\right) \left(\frac{4x^2}{y^2}\right)
$$

$$
K_{sp} = \frac{108x^5}{y^5}
$$

The required ratio is \(\frac{[A^{-3}]}{K_{sp}}\):

$$
\text{Ratio} = \frac{\frac{2x}{y}}{\frac{108x^5}{y^5}}
$$

$$
\text{Ratio} = \frac{2x}{y} \times \frac{y^5}{108x^5}
$$

$$
\text{Ratio} = \frac{2 \cdot y^4}{108 \cdot x^4}
$$

$$
\text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54} \frac{y^4}{x^4}
$$

Thus, the ratio is \(\frac{1}{54} \frac{y^4}{x^4}\).

questions.question: Consider two Group IV metal ions $X^{2+}$ and $Y^{2+}$. A solution containing $0.01$ M $X^{2+}$ and $0.01$ M $Y^{2+}$ is saturated with $H_{2}S$. The pH at which the metal sulphide $YS$ will form as a precipitate is _______ (Nearest integer) (Given : K_{$\mathrm{sp}$}(XS)=1\times $10^{-22} \text{ at } 25^{$\circ$}$C, K_{$\mathrm{sp}$}(YS)=4\times $10^{-16} \text{ at } 25^{$\circ$}$C, [$H_{2}$S] = 0.1M$\text{ in solution, } K_{a1}$ \times $K_{a2}$ ($H_{2}$S) = 1.0 \times $10^{-21}$, $\log$ 2 = 0.30, $\log$ 3 = 0.48, $\log$ 5 = 0.70)
questions.explanation:
$$
XS(s) \rightleftharpoons X^{+2}(aq.) + S^{2-}(aq.)
$$

$$
[X^{+2}][S^{2-}] \ge K_{\mathrm{sp}}(XS)
$$

$$
[S^{2-}] \ge \frac{1\times 10^{-22}}{0.01} = 10^{-20}
$$

$$
YS(s) \rightleftharpoons Y^{+2}(aq) + S^{2-}(aq)
$$

$$
[Y^{+2}][S^{2-}] \ge K_{\mathrm{sp}}(YS)
$$

$$
[S^{2-}] \ge \frac{4\times 10^{-16}}{10^{-2}} = 4 \times 10^{-14}
$$

For YS to precipitate, the minimum \([S^{2-}]\) required is \(4 \times 10^{-14}\). This is a higher concentration than for XS, so YS will precipitate first.

$$
H_{2}S(aq) \rightleftharpoons 2H^{+}(aq) + S^{2-}(aq)
$$

$$
\frac{[S^{2-}][H^{+}]^{2}}{[H_{2}S]} = K_{a1} \times K_{a2} = 1\times 10^{-21}
$$

$$
[S^{2-}] = \frac{1\times 10^{-21} \times [H_{2}S]}{[H^{+}]^{2}}
$$

For YS to precipitate, we need \([S^{2-}] \ge 4 \times 10^{-14}\).

$$
\frac{1\times 10^{-21} \times [H_{2}S]}{[H^{+}]^{2}} \ge 4 \times 10^{-14}
$$

Given \([H_{2}S] = 0.1\) M:

$$
\frac{1\times 10^{-21} \times 0.1}{[H^{+}]^{2}} \ge 4 \times 10^{-14}
$$

$$
\frac{1\times 10^{-22}}{[H^{+}]^{2}} \ge 4 \times 10^{-14}
$$

$$
[H^{+}]^{2} \le \frac{1\times 10^{-22}}{4 \times 10^{-14}}
$$

$$
[H^{+}]^{2} \le \frac{1}{4} \times 10^{-8}
$$

$$
[H^{+}] \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} \times 10^{-8}}
$$

$$
[H^{+}] \le \frac{1}{2} \times 10^{-4}
$$

$$
[H^{+}] \le 0.5 \times 10^{-4}
$$

$$
[H^{+}] \le 5 \times 10^{-5}
$$

To find pH, we take the negative logarithm:

$$
pH = -\log[H^{+}]
$$

$$
pH \ge -\log(5 \times 10^{-5})
$$

$$
pH \ge -(\log 5 + \log 10^{-5})
$$

$$
pH \ge -(\log 5 - 5)
$$

Using given \(\log 5 = 0.70\):

$$
pH \ge -(0.70 - 5)
$$

$$
pH \ge -(-4.30)
$$

$$
pH \ge 4.30
$$

The pH at which YS will form as a precipitate is \(4.30\). The question asks for the nearest integer.

questions.question: Consider a weak base 'B' of $pK_{b} = 5.699$. 'x' mL of $0.02$ M HCl and 'y' mL of $0.02$ M weak base 'B' are mixed to make $100$ mL of a buffer of pH $9$ at $25^{\circ}C$. The values of 'x' and 'y' respectively are: [Given: $\log 2 = 0.3010$, $\log 3 = 0.4771$, $\log 5 = 0.699$]
questions.explanation:
The reaction between HCl (strong acid) and weak base B is:

$$
\text{HCl} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{BH}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}
$$

Initial moles (M \(\times\) mL):

$$
\text{HCl}: 0.02x \quad \text{B}: 0.02y
$$

Since HCl is a strong acid and B is a weak base, they will react. For a buffer solution, some weak base must remain, so HCl is the limiting reactant.

Moles after reaction (at \(t_f\)):

$$
\text{HCl}: 0 \quad \text{B}: 0.02y - 0.02x \quad \text{BH}^{+}: 0.02x
$$

The solution is a buffer of pH \(9\) at \(25^{\circ}C\). Therefore, \(pOH = 14 - pH = 14 - 9 = 5\).

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer:

$$
pOH = pK_{b} + \log \frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]}
$$

Substitute the given values:

$$
5 = 5.699 + \log \frac{0.02x}{0.02y - 0.02x}
$$

$$
5 = 5.699 + \log \frac{x}{y-x}
$$

$$
\log \frac{x}{y-x} = 5 - 5.699 = -0.699
$$

We are given \(\log 5 = 0.699\). Therefore, \(-0.699 = \log \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\).

$$
\frac{x}{y-x} = \frac{1}{5}
$$

$$
5x = y - x
$$

$$
6x = y \quad \ldots (1)
$$

The total volume of the buffer is \(100\) mL:

$$
x + y = 100 \quad \ldots (2)
$$

Substitute (1) into (2):

$$
x + 6x = 100
$$

$$
7x = 100
$$

$$
x = \frac{100}{7} \approx 14.2857 \text{ mL}
$$

Now find y:

$$
y = 6x = 6 \times \frac{100}{7} = \frac{600}{7} \approx 85.7143 \text{ mL}
$$

Comparing these values with the given options, option (3) (C) matches the calculated values (rounded to one decimal place).

questions.question: At 25°C, 20.0 mL of 0.2 M weak monoprotic acid HX is titrated against 0.2 M NaOH. The pH of the solution (a) at the start of the titration (when NaOH has not been added) and (b) when 10 mL of NaOH is added respectively, are : Given : $K_a = 5 \times 10^{-4}$, $pK_a = 3.3$, $\alpha \ll 1$
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

At the start of the titration, we have a weak monoprotic acid HX with concentration \(c = 0.2\) M and \(pK_a = 3.3\).

The pH of a weak acid solution is given by the formula:

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[pK_a - \log c]
$$

We are given \(pK_a = 3.3\) and \(c = 0.2\) M. We also know that \(pK_a = -\log K_a = -\log(5 \times 10^{-4}) = 4 - \log 5\).

Substituting the values into the formula:

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[(4 - \log 5) - \log 0.2]
$$

Since \(\log 0.2 = \log(1/5) = -\log 5\), we can simplify the expression:

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[4 - \log 5 + \log 5]
$$

$$
pH = \frac{1}{2}[4]
$$

$$
pH = 2.0
$$

Initial moles of HX = \(20.0 \text{ mL} \times 0.2 \text{ M} = 4.0 \text{ mmole}\)

Moles of NaOH added = \(10.0 \text{ mL} \times 0.2 \text{ M} = 2.0 \text{ mmole}\)

The reaction between the weak acid (HX) and the strong base (NaOH) is:

$$
HX + NaOH \rightarrow NaA + H_2O
$$

Let's track the moles before and after the reaction:

• Initial moles of HX = 4.0 mmole
• Initial moles of NaOH = 2.0 mmole
• Initial moles of NaA = 0 mmole

Since NaOH is the limiting reagent, 2.0 mmole of HX will react with 2.0 mmole of NaOH to form 2.0 mmole of NaA.

• Moles of HX remaining = \(4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0 \text{ mmole}\)
• Moles of NaOH remaining = \(2.0 - 2.0 = 0 \text{ mmole}\)
• Moles of NaA formed = \(2.0 \text{ mmole}\)

The solution now contains a weak acid (HX) and its conjugate base (NaA) in equal amounts, forming an acidic buffer. We can use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:

$$
pH = pK_a + \log \frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}
$$

Substituting the values (moles can be used directly as volume cancels out):

$$
pH = 3.3 + \log \frac{2.0 \text{ mmole}}{2.0 \text{ mmole}}
$$

$$
pH = 3.3 + \log 1
$$

$$
pH = 3.3 + 0
$$

$$
pH = 3.3
$$

questions.question: 19.5 g of fluoro acetic acid (molar mass = 78 g mol$^{-1}$) is dissolved in 500g of water at 298 K. The depression in the freezing point of water was 1°C. What is $K_a$ of fluoro acetic acid ? (For water, $K_f = 1.86$ K kg mol$^{-1}$). Assume molarity and molality to have same values.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given: mass of fluoro acetic acid = 19.5 g, molar mass = 78 g mol\(^{-1}\), mass of water = 500 g = 0.5 kg, \(\Delta T_f = 1^\circ C\), \(K_f = 1.86\) K kg mol\(^{-1}\).

$$
\text{Number of moles of fluoro acetic acid} = \frac{19.5}{78} = \frac{1}{4} \text{ mole}
$$

$$
\text{Molality (m)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}} = \frac{1/4}{0.5} = \frac{1}{2} \text{ mol kg}^{-1}
$$

The depression in freezing point is given by:

$$
\Delta T_{f} = iK_{f}m
$$

Substitute the given values:

$$
1 = i \times 1.86 \times \frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
i = \frac{2}{1.86} \approx 1.075
$$

Fluoro acetic acid (HA) is a weak acid and dissociates as HA \(\rightleftharpoons\) H\(^{+}\) + A\(^{-}\). Thus, the number of ions produced (n) is 2.

The van't Hoff factor (i) is related to the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) by the formula:

$$
i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha
$$

For this dissociation:

$$
i = 1 + (2-1)\alpha = 1 + \alpha
$$

Now, calculate \(\alpha\):

$$
\alpha = i - 1 = \frac{2}{1.86} - 1 \approx 1.075 - 1 = 0.075
$$

The acid dissociation constant (\(K_a\)) for a weak acid is given by:

$$
K_{a} = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}
$$

Given that molarity and molality are assumed to be the same, we use \(C = m = \frac{1}{2}\).

$$
K_{a} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{(0.075)^2}{(1-0.075)}
$$

$$
K_{a} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{0.005625}{0.925}
$$

$$
K_{a} = 0.5 \times 0.006081 \approx 0.00304
$$

$$
K_{a} \approx 3 \times 10^{-3}
$$

questions.question: Given below are two statement : Statement (I) : Aqueous solution of ammonium carbonate is basic Statement (II) : Acidic/basic nature of salt solution of a salt of weak acid and weak base depends on $K_{a}$ and $K_{b}$ value of acid and the base forming it. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Ammonium carbonate, \((NH_{4})_{2}CO_{3}\), is a salt formed from a weak acid (carbonic acid, \(H_{2}CO_{3}\)) and a weak base (ammonium hydroxide, \(NH_{4}OH\)).

For such salts, the nature of the aqueous solution depends on the relative strengths of the weak acid and weak base, specifically their dissociation constants, \(K_{a}\) and \(K_{b}\).

The relevant dissociation constants are:

$$
K_{a}(H_{2}CO_{3}) = 4.3 \times 10^{-7}
$$

$$
K_{b}(NH_{4}OH) = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}
$$

Since \(K_{b} > K_{a}\), the hydrolysis of the ammonium ion \((NH_{4}^{+})\) is less significant than the hydrolysis of the carbonate ion \((CO_{3}^{2-})\). The solution will be basic.

Therefore, Statement I is correct.

The acidic/basic nature (pH) of a salt solution formed from a weak acid and a weak base is determined by the relative strengths of the acid and base. The pH of such a solution can be calculated using the formula:

$$
pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_{a} - pK_{b})
$$

This formula clearly shows that the pH, and thus the acidic or basic nature, depends on the \(pK_{a}\) (which is related to \(K_{a}\)) of the weak acid and the \(pK_{b}\) (which is related to \(K_{b}\)) of the weak base that formed the salt.

Therefore, Statement II is correct.

Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

questions.question: 25 mL of silver nitrate solution (1M) is added dropwise to 25 mL of potassium iodide (1.05 M) solution. The ion(s) present in very small quantity in the solution is/are
questions.explanation:
Given:

Volume of \(AgNO_{3}\) solution = 25 mL

Concentration of \(AgNO_{3}\) solution = 1 M

Volume of \(KI\) solution = 25 mL

Concentration of \(KI\) solution = 1.05 M

Moles of \(AgNO_{3}\) = Volume \(\times\) Concentration = \(25 \text{ mL} \times 1 \text{ M} = 0.025 \text{ L} \times 1 \text{ mol/L} = 0.025 \text{ mol}\)

Moles of \(KI\) = Volume \(\times\) Concentration = \(25 \text{ mL} \times 1.05 \text{ M} = 0.025 \text{ L} \times 1.05 \text{ mol/L} = 0.02625 \text{ mol}\)

The reaction between silver nitrate and potassium iodide is:

$$
AgNO_{3}(aq) + KI(aq) \rightarrow AgI(s) + KNO_{3}(aq)
$$

Or, in ionic form:

$$
Ag^{+}(aq) + I^{-}(aq) \rightarrow AgI(s)
$$

Initial moles:

$$
Ag^{+}: 0.025 \text{ mol}
$$

$$
I^{-}: 0.02625 \text{ mol}
$$

Since \(Ag^{+}\) is the limiting reactant, it will be almost completely consumed to form \(AgI\) precipitate. \(I^{-}\) is in excess.

After reaction:

$$
Ag^{+}: \approx 0 \text{ mol (very small quantity due to low solubility of AgI)}
$$

$$
I^{-}: 0.02625 - 0.025 = 0.00125 \text{ mol (excess)}
$$

The solubility of \(AgI\) is very low, meaning that the concentration of \(Ag^{+}\) ions in equilibrium with the solid \(AgI\) will be extremely small. Although there is an excess of \(I^{-}\) ions, the question asks for ions present in "very small quantity". In the context of solubility equilibrium, both \(Ag^{+}\) and \(I^{-}\) ions that are in equilibrium with the solid \(AgI\) are present in very small quantities. The common ion effect from the excess \(I^{-}\) further suppresses the \(Ag^{+}\) concentration.

Therefore, \([Ag^{+}]\) will be very small. The \([I^{-}]\) concentration from the dissolution of \(AgI\) is also very small, but the total \([I^{-}]\) concentration is dominated by the excess \(I^{-}\) (0.00125 mol in 50 mL total volume, which is 0.025 M). However, following the provided solution's reasoning, it considers both \(Ag^{+}\) and \(I^{-}\) to be in very small quantities, likely referring to their equilibrium concentrations from the precipitate.

On adding \(AgNO_{3}\) into \(KI\), \(AgI\) will form and solubility of \(AgI\) is very low. So, \([Ag^{+}]\) and \([I^{-}]\) will be present in very small quantity.

questions.question: The total number of correct statements, regarding the nucleic acids is • A. RNA is regarded as the reserve of genetic information • B. DNA molecule self-duplicates during cell division • C. DNA synthesizes proteins in the cell • D. The message for the synthesis of particular proteins is present in DNA • E. Identical DNA strands are transferred to daughter cells.
questions.explanation:
Let's evaluate each statement:

• A. RNA is regarded as the reserve of genetic information. This statement is **False**. DNA is the primary carrier of genetic information in most organisms.
• B. DNA molecule self-duplicates during cell division. This statement is **True**. This process is called replication.
• C. DNA synthesizes proteins in the cell. This statement is **False**. The process of protein synthesis (translation) is carried out by ribosomes using information from mRNA.
• D. The message for the synthesis of particular proteins is present in DNA. This statement is **True**. The genetic code in DNA is transcribed into mRNA, which then directs protein synthesis.
• E. Identical DNA strands are transferred to daughter cells. This statement is **True**. After replication, the identical DNA molecules are segregated into the two daughter cells during cell division.

The correct statements are B, D, and E. Therefore, the total number of correct statements is 3.

questions.question: The first and second ionization constants of $H_{2}X$ are $2.5 \times 10^{-8}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-13}$ respectively. The concentration of $X^{2-}$ in $0.1$ M $H_{2}X$ solution is $ \_\_\_\_\_ \times 10^{-15}$ M. (Nearest Integer)
questions.explanation:
$$
H_{2}X \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + HX^{-}
$$

Initial concentrations: \(0.1\) M \(H_{2}X\), \(0\) M \(H^{+}\), \(0\) M \(HX^{-}\)

At equilibrium: \(0.1-x\) M \(H_{2}X\), \(x+y\) M \(H^{+}\), \(x-y\) M \(HX^{-}\)

$$
K_{a_{1}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-8} = \frac{(x+y)(x-y)}{0.1-x}
$$

$$
HX^{-} \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + X^{2-}
$$

Initial concentrations: \(x-y\) M \(HX^{-}\), \(x+y\) M \(H^{+}\), \(0\) M \(X^{2-}\)

At equilibrium: \(x-y\) M \(HX^{-}\), \(x+y\) M \(H^{+}\), \(y\) M \(X^{2-}\)

$$
K_{a_{2}} = 1 \times 10^{-13} = \frac{(x+y)(y)}{x-y}
$$

Since \(K_{a_{1}} \gg K_{a_{2}}\), we can assume that the contribution of \(y\) (from the second ionization) to the total \(H^{+}\) concentration and the change in \(HX^{-}\) concentration is much smaller than \(x\) (from the first ionization). Therefore, we can approximate:

$$
x+y \approx x \text{ and } x-y \approx x
$$

$$
1 \times 10^{-13} = \frac{(x)(y)}{x}
$$

$$
y = 10^{-13}
$$

The concentration of \(X^{2-}\) is \(y\).

$$
[X^{2-}] = 10^{-13}
$$

To express this in the format \( \_\_\_\_\_ \times 10^{-15}\) M, we convert:

$$
[X^{2-}] = 100 \times 10^{-15}
$$

questions.question: pH of water is 7 at 25°C. If water is heated to 80°C, it's pH will :

questions.question: Which of the following mixture gives a buffer solution with $pH = 9.25$ ? Given : $pK_{b} \, (NH_{4}OH) = 4.75$
questions.explanation:
Given \(pH = 9.25\).

We know that \(pH + pOH = 14\).

$$
pOH = 14 - pH = 14 - 9.25 = 4.75
$$

For a basic buffer, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is:

$$
pOH = pK_{b} + \log \frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]}
$$

Substitute the given \(pK_{b}\) and calculated \(pOH\):

$$
4.75 = 4.75 + \log \frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]}
$$

This implies:

$$
\log \frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]} = 0
$$

$$
\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]} = 10^0 = 1
$$

Therefore, for the buffer solution to have \(pH = 9.25\), the milimoles of salt formed must be equal to the milimoles of the remaining weak base.

Consider the mixture in Option B (2): \(0.2M \, NH_{4}OH \, (0.5 \, L) + 0.1M \, HCl \, (0.5 \, L)\)

The reaction is:

$$
NH_{4}OH \, + \, HCl \, \rightarrow \, NH_{4}Cl \, + \, H_{2}O
$$

Initial milimoles:

$$
\text{Milimoles of } NH_{4}OH = 0.2 \, M \times 0.5 \, L = 0.1 \, mol = 100 \, \text{mmole}
$$

$$
\text{Milimoles of } HCl = 0.1 \, M \times 0.5 \, L = 0.05 \, mol = 50 \, \text{mmole}
$$

Since \(HCl\) is the limiting reactant, it will react completely.

After reaction:

$$
\text{Remaining } NH_{4}OH = 100 \, \text{mmole} - 50 \, \text{mmole} = 50 \, \text{mmole} \, (\text{Base})
$$

$$
\text{Formed } NH_{4}Cl = 50 \, \text{mmole} \, (\text{Salt})
$$

In this mixture, \(\text{milimoles of } NH_{4}OH = \text{milimoles of } NH_{4}Cl = 50 \, \text{mmole}\).

Since \([\text{Salt}] = [\text{Base}]\), this mixture forms a buffer with \(pOH = pK_{b} = 4.75\), which corresponds to \(pH = 14 - 4.75 = 9.25\).

Option B (2) gives a buffer solution with \(pH = 9.25\).

questions.question: If the $pK_{a}$ of lactic acid is 5, then the pH of 0.005M calcium lactate solution at 25°C is ______ $\times 10^{-1}$ (Nearest integer) Lactic acid structure:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Calcium lactate dissociates in water as follows:

$$
Ca(Lac)_{2} \longrightarrow Ca^{+2} + 2Lac^{-}
$$

Given the initial concentration of calcium lactate is \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) M. From the stoichiometry of the dissociation, the concentration of the lactate ion (Lac\(^{-}\)) is:

$$
[Lac^{-}] = 2 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 10^{-2} \text{ M}
$$

Calcium lactate is a salt formed from a strong base (calcium hydroxide, \(Ca(OH)_{2}\)) and a weak acid (lactic acid). The pH of such a solution (salt of strong base and weak acid) is given by the formula:

$$
pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2} pK_{a} + \frac{1}{2} \log c
$$

Where \(pK_{a}\) is the acid dissociation constant of the weak acid and \(c\) is the concentration of the conjugate base (lactate ion).

Given \(pK_{a} = 5\) and we found \(c = [Lac^{-}] = 10^{-2}\) M. Substitute these values into the pH formula:

$$
pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2} \times 5 + \frac{1}{2} \log (10^{-2})
$$

$$
pH = 7 + 2.5 + \frac{1}{2} \times (-2)
$$

$$
pH = 7 + 2.5 - 1
$$

$$
pH = 8.5
$$

The question asks for the pH in the format \(X \times 10^{-1}\) (Nearest integer). We have calculated \(pH = 8.5\).

$$
8.5 = 85 \times 10^{-1}
$$

Therefore, the value of \(X\) is 85.

questions.question: A weak acid HA has degree of dissociation x. Which option gives the correct expression of $pH - pK_{a}$ ?
questions.explanation:
The dissociation of the weak acid HA is represented by the equilibrium:

$$
HA \rightleftharpoons H^{\oplus} + A^{\ominus}
$$

Let the initial concentration of HA be 'a'. The concentrations at equilibrium are:

The acid dissociation constant, \(K_{a}\), is given by:

$$
K_{a} = \frac{[H^{\oplus}][A^{\ominus}]}{[HA]} = \frac{(ax)(ax)}{a(1-x)} = \frac{ax^2}{1-x}
$$

From the table, the hydrogen ion concentration is \([H^{+}] = ax\). The expression for \(K_{a}\) can be written as:

$$
K_{a} = (ax) \cdot \frac{x}{1-x} = [H^{+}] \frac{x}{1-x}
$$

Taking the negative logarithm on both sides:

$$
-\log(K_{a}) = -\log([H^{+}]) - \log\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)
$$

Using the definitions \(pK_{a} = -\log(K_{a})\) and \(pH = -\log([H^{+}])\):

$$
pK_{a} = pH - \log\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)
$$

Rearranging the equation to find the expression for \(pH - pK_{a}\):

$$
pH - pK_{a} = \log\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)
$$

questions.question: Molar conductivity of a weak acid HQ of concentration 0.18 M was found to be 1/30 of the molar conductivity of another weak acid HZ with concentration of 0.02 M. If $\lambda_{Q^-}^0$ happened to be equal with $\lambda_{Z^-}^0$, then the difference of the $p K_a$ values of the two weak acids ($p K_a(HQ) - p K_a(HZ)$) is ______ (Nearest integer). [Given : degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) $\ll$ 1 for both weak acids, $\lambda^0$ : limiting molar conductivity of ions]
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For a weak acid, the acid dissociation constant \(K_a\) is given by Ostwald's dilution law as \(K_a = C\alpha^2\), where \(C\) is the concentration and \(\alpha\) is the degree of dissociation.

The degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) can also be expressed in terms of molar conductivity as \(\alpha = \frac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_m^\infty}\), where \(\lambda_m\) is the molar conductivity at a given concentration and \(\lambda_m^\infty\) is the limiting molar conductivity.

$$
K_a(HQ) = C_1 \alpha_1^2
$$

$$
\alpha_1 = \frac{\lambda_m(HQ)}{\lambda_m^\infty(HQ)}
$$

$$
K_a(HZ) = C_2 \alpha_2^2
$$

$$
\alpha_2 = \frac{\lambda_m(HZ)}{\lambda_m^\infty(HZ)}
$$

Given that \(\lambda_{Q^-}^0 = \lambda_{Z^-}^0\). Since \(\lambda_m^\infty(HQ) = \lambda_{H^+}^0 + \lambda_{Q^-}^0\) and \(\lambda_m^\infty(HZ) = \lambda_{H^+}^0 + \lambda_{Z^-}^0\), it implies that \(\lambda_m^\infty(HQ) = \lambda_m^\infty(HZ)\). Let's denote this as \(\lambda_m^\infty\).

Now, let's take the ratio of the dissociation constants:

$$
\frac{K_a(HQ)}{K_a(HZ)} = \frac{C_1 \alpha_1^2}{C_2 \alpha_2^2} = \frac{C_1}{C_2} \left(\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2}\right)^2
$$

Substitute the expressions for \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\):

$$
\frac{K_a(HQ)}{K_a(HZ)} = \frac{C_1}{C_2} \left(\frac{\lambda_m(HQ) / \lambda_m^\infty(HQ)}{\lambda_m(HZ) / \lambda_m^\infty(HZ)}\right)^2
$$

Since \(\lambda_m^\infty(HQ) = \lambda_m^\infty(HZ)\), they cancel out:

$$
\frac{K_a(HQ)}{K_a(HZ)} = \frac{C_1}{C_2} \left(\frac{\lambda_m(HQ)}{\lambda_m(HZ)}\right)^2
$$

Given values:

\(C_1 = 0.18\) M

\(C_2 = 0.02\) M

\(\lambda_m(HQ) = \frac{1}{30} \lambda_m(HZ)\)

Substitute these values into the ratio equation:

$$
\frac{K_a(HQ)}{K_a(HZ)} = \frac{0.18}{0.02} \left(\frac{1/30 \lambda_m(HZ)}{\lambda_m(HZ)}\right)^2
$$

$$
\frac{K_a(HQ)}{K_a(HZ)} = 9 \times \left(\frac{1}{30}\right)^2 = 9 \times \frac{1}{900} = \frac{1}{100}
$$

Now, we need to find the difference in \(p K_a\) values:

\(p K_a(HQ) - p K_a(HZ) = -\log K_a(HQ) - (-\log K_a(HZ))\)

\(= \log K_a(HZ) - \log K_a(HQ) = \log \left(\frac{K_a(HZ)}{K_a(HQ)}\right)\)

Since \(\frac{K_a(HQ)}{K_a(HZ)} = \frac{1}{100}\), then \(\frac{K_a(HZ)}{K_a(HQ)} = 100\).

$$
p K_a(HQ) - p K_a(HZ) = \log(100) = 2
$$

$$
2\times10^{-10} = x^{2} - 2\times10^{-5}
$$
$$
x^{2} = 2\times10^{-5} + 2\times10^{-10}
$$
$$
x^{2} = 2\times10^{-5}(1 + 10^{-5})
$$
Since \(10^{-5}\) is very small, \(1 + 10^{-5} \approx 1\).
x^{2} \approx 2\times10^{-5}
$$
x = \sqrt{2\times10^{-5}} = \sqrt{20\times10^{-6}} = \sqrt{20}\times10^{-3}
$$
x \approx 4.472\times10^{-3}
Comparing with the given solubility \(Y\times10^{-3}\) mol \(L^{-1}\):
$$
Y = 4.47
$$

questions.question: At 25$^\circ$C, the concentration of $H^+$ ions in $1.00 \times 10^{-3}$ M aqueous solution of a weak monobasic acid having acid dissociation constant $(K_a) = 4.00 \times 10^{-11}$ is $X \times 10^{-7}$ M. The value of $X$ is ________. Use: Ionic product of water $(K_w) = 1.00 \times 10^{-14}$ at 25$^\circ$C
questions.explanation:
Because concentration of \(H^+\) from weak acid is less we need to consider self ionization of \(H_2O\) also.
HX(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^+(aq) + X^-(aq)
10^{-3}-x \quad x+y \quad x
H_2O(l) \rightleftharpoons H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq)
x+y \quad y
Approximation : \((10^{-3}-x) \approx 10^{-3}\)
$$
\frac{x(x+y)}{10^{-3}} = K_a = 4 \times 10^{-11} \quad \ldots\ldots(1)
$$
$$
y(x+y) = K_w = 10^{-14} \quad \ldots\ldots(2)
$$
Add (1) + (2)
$$
(x+y)^2 = 5 \times 10^{-14}
$$
$$
x+y = [H^+] = \sqrt{5} \times 10^{-7}
$$
$$
x = \sqrt{5} = 2.236
$$

questions.question: The solubility of barium iodate in an aqueous solution prepared by mixing 200 mL of 0.010 M barium nitrate with 100 mL of 0.10 M sodium iodate is $X \times 10^{-6}$ mol dm$^{-3}$. The value of $X$ is ______. Use: Solubility product constant ($K_{sp}$) of barium iodate = $1.58 \times 10^{-9}$
questions.explanation:
The reaction between barium nitrate and sodium iodate is:
$$
\text{Ba(NO}_3\text{)}_2\text{(aq)} + 2\text{NaIO}_3\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Ba(IO}_3\text{)}_2\text{(s)} + 2\text{NaNO}_3\text{(aq)}
$$
Initial moles:
• Moles of \(\text{Ba(NO}_3\text{)}_2\) = \(200 \text{ mL} \times 0.010 \text{ M} = 2 \text{ mmol}\)
• Moles of \(\text{NaIO}_3\) = \(100 \text{ mL} \times 0.10 \text{ M} = 10 \text{ mmol}\)
Stoichiometry check for limiting reagent:
• For \(\text{Ba(NO}_3\text{)}_2\): \(2 \text{ mmol} / 1 = 2\)
• For \(\text{NaIO}_3\): \(10 \text{ mmol} / 2 = 5\)
Since \(2 < 5\), \(\text{Ba(NO}_3\text{)}_2\) is the limiting reagent (LR).
After the reaction:
• \(\text{Ba(NO}_3\text{)}_2\) consumed = \(2 \text{ mmol}\)
• \(\text{NaIO}_3\) consumed = \(2 \times 2 \text{ mmol} = 4 \text{ mmol}\)
• \(\text{NaIO}_3\) remaining = \(10 - 4 = 6 \text{ mmol}\)
• \(\text{Ba(IO}_3\text{)}_2\) formed = \(2 \text{ mmol}\)
$$
Total volume of the solution = \(200 \text{ mL} + 100 \text{ mL} = 300 \text{ mL}\)
$$
Concentration of \(\text{IO}_3^{-}\) from remaining \(\text{NaIO}_3\):
$$
[\text{NaIO}_3] = \frac{6 \text{ mmol}}{300 \text{ mL}} = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ M}
$$
Now consider the solubility equilibrium of \(\text{Ba(IO}_3\text{)}_2\):
$$
\text{Ba(IO}_3\text{)}_2\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ba}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{IO}_3^{-}\text{(aq)}
$$
Let 's' be the solubility of \(\text{Ba(IO}_3\text{)}_2\).
• \([\text{Ba}^{2+}] = s\)
• \([\text{IO}_3^{-}] = (2 \times 10^{-2}) + 2s\) (from common ion effect)
The solubility product constant expression is:
$$
K_{sp} = [\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{IO}_3^{-}]^2
$$
Substitute the values:
$$
1.58 \times 10^{-9} = s \times (2 \times 10^{-2} + 2s)^2
$$
Since \(K_{sp}\) is very small, we can assume that \(2s \ll 2 \times 10^{-2}\). Therefore, \((2 \times 10^{-2} + 2s) \approx 2 \times 10^{-2}\).
$$
1.58 \times 10^{-9} = s \times (2 \times 10^{-2})^2
$$
$$
1.58 \times 10^{-9} = s \times (4 \times 10^{-4})
$$
$$
s = \frac{1.58 \times 10^{-9}}{4 \times 10^{-4}}
$$
$$
s = 0.395 \times 10^{-5}
$$
$$
s = 3.95 \times 10^{-6} \text{ M}
$$
The solubility is given as \(X \times 10^{-6}\) mol dm\(^{-3}\).
$$
Comparing with our calculated solubility, \(X = 3.95\).
$$

questions.question: A solution of 0.1 M weak base (B) is titrated with 0.1 M of a strong acid (HA). The variation of pH of the solution with the volume of HA added is shown in the figure below. What is the $pK_{b}$ of the base? The neutralization reaction is given by $B+HA \to BH^{+}+A^{-}$.
questions.explanation:
### Solution for \(pK_{b}\) of the weak base


### Method 1: Using pH at equivalence point

The neutralization reaction is given as:
B + HA \to BH^{+} + A^{-}
Given initial concentration of weak base (B) is 0.1 M and its volume is V ml. Strong acid (HA) concentration is also 0.1 M. At the equivalence point, the volume of HA added will be V ml (since concentrations are equal).
$$
Moles of \(BH^{+}\) formed at equivalence point \(= 0.1 \times V\) mmol.
$$
$$
Total volume at equivalence point \(= V + V = 2V\) ml.
$$
$$
[BH^{+}] = \frac{0.1 V}{2 V} = 0.05 M
$$
From the titration curve, the pH at the equivalence point (the steepest part of the curve) is approximately 6 to 6.28.
For the titration of a weak base with a strong acid, the pH at the equivalence point is given by:
$$
pH = 7 - \frac{1}{2} [pK_{b} + \log [BH^{+}]]
$$
Substituting the values:
$$
pH = 7 - \frac{1}{2} [pK_{b} + \log 0.05]
$$
Using the pH range of 6 to 6.28:
$$
6 = 7 - \frac{1}{2} [pK_{b} + \log 0.05] \implies 1 = \frac{1}{2} [pK_{b} - 1.30] \implies 2 = pK_{b} - 1.30 \implies pK_{b} = 3.30
$$
$$
6.28 = 7 - \frac{1}{2} [pK_{b} + \log 0.05] \implies 0.72 = \frac{1}{2} [pK_{b} - 1.30] \implies 1.44 = pK_{b} - 1.30 \implies pK_{b} = 2.74
$$
$$
So, \(pK_{b}\) is in the range of 2.74 to 3.30. The solution states a possible range of \(pK_{b} = 2.30 - 2.80\).
$$

### Method 2: Using the half-equivalence point (Solution-2)

From the graph, the reaction is complete (equivalence point) at \(V = 6\) ml of HA added.
The half-equivalence point is at \(V = 3\) ml of HA added.
At the half-equivalence point (3 ml HA), the pH from the graph is approximately 11.
$$
At the half-equivalence point of a weak base titration, \([B] = [BH^{+}]\), and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a base is \(pOH = pK_{b} + \log \frac{[BH^{+}]}{[B]}\).
$$
Since \([B] = [BH^{+}]\) at half-equivalence point, \(\log \frac{[BH^{+}]}{[B]} = \log 1 = 0\).
Therefore, at the half-equivalence point, \(pOH = pK_{b}\).
Given pH = 11 at half-equivalence point, then \(pOH = 14 - pH = 14 - 11 = 3\).
$$
pK_{b} = 3
$$
The \(pK_{b}\) of the base is 3.

questions.question:
Dilution processes of different aqueous solutions, with water, are given in LIST-I. The effects of dilution of the solution on $[H^+]$ are given in LIST-II.
(Note : degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) of weak acid and weak base is $\ll 1$; degree of hydrolysis of salt $\ll 1$; $[H^+]$ represents the concentration of $H^+$ ions)
Match each process given in LIST-I with one or more effect(s) in LIST-II. the correct option is

items.label: P
items.text: (10 mL of 0.1 M NaOH + 20 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid) diluted to 60 mL

items.label: Q
items.text: (20 mL of 0.1 M NaOH + 20 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid) diluted to 80 mL

items.label: R
items.text: (20 mL of 0.1 M HCl + 20 mL of 0.1 M ammonia solution) diluted to 80 mL

items.label: S
items.text: 10 mL saturated solution of $\text{Ni(OH)}_2$ in equilibrium with excess solid $\text{Ni(OH)}_2$ is diluted to 20 mL (solid $\text{Ni(OH)}_2$ is still present after dilution).
the value of $[H^+]$ does not change on dilution
the value of $[H^+]$ changes to half of its initial value on dilution
the value of $[H^+]$ changes to two times of its initial value on dilution
the value of $[H^+]$ changes to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ times of its initial value on dilution
the value of $[H^+]$ changes to $\sqrt{2}$ times of its initial value on dilution

questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### (P) Calculation

\(\text{NaOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \to \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
M.Mole: 1 (from 10 mL of 0.1 M NaOH) and 2 (from 20 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid)
Now solution contains 1 m.mole \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) & 1 m.mole \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\) in 30 ml solution.
It is a Buffer solution
\(\therefore\) \([H^+]\) does not change with dilution.
So, P \(\to\) 1

### (Q) Calculation

\(\text{NaOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \to \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
M.Mole: 2 (from 20 mL of 0.1 M NaOH) and 2 (from 20 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid)
Now solution contain 2 m.mole of \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\) in 40 ml solution (salt of weak acid strong base)
$$
[H^+]_{\text{initial}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w K_a}{C}}
$$
$$
Now on dilution upto 80 ml, new conc. becomes \(\frac{C}{2}\).
$$
$$
\therefore [H^+]_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w K_a}{C/2}} = [H^+]_{\text{initial}} \times \sqrt{2}
$$
So, Q \(\to\) 5

### (R) Calculation

\(\text{HCl} + \text{NH}_3 \to \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\)
M.Mole: 2 (from 20 mL of 0.1 M HCl) and 2 (from 20 mL of 0.1 M ammonia solution)
Now solution contain 2 m.mole of \(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\) in 40 ml solution (salt of SA & WB)
$$
[H^+]_{\text{initial}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w C}{K_b}}
$$
$$
Now on dilution upto 80 ml, new conc. becomes \(\frac{C}{2}\).
$$
$$
\therefore [H^+]_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_w C/2}{K_b}} = \frac{[H^+]_{\text{initial}}}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
So, R \(\to\) 4

### (S) Calculation

\(\text{Ni(OH)}_2 \text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-\\ \therefore\) it is sparingly soluble salt
\(\therefore\) on dilution \([\text{OH}^-]\) conc. in saturated solution of \(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) remains constant.
\(\therefore [H^+]_{\text{new}} = [H^+]_{\text{initial}}\)
So, S \(\to\) 1

questions.question: An acidified solution of $0.05$ M $Zn^{2+}$ is saturated with $0.1$ M $H_{2}S$. What is the minimum molar concentration (M) of $H^{+}$ required to prevent the precipitation of $ZnS$ ? Use $K_{\mathrm{sp}} (ZnS) = 1.25 \times 10^{-22}$ and Overall dissociation constant of $H_{2}S$ , $K_{\mathrm{NET}} = K_{1}K_{2} = 1 \times 10^{-21}$
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Calculate the maximum allowed sulfide ion concentration to prevent precipitation.

For precipitation (ppt) of \(ZnS\), the ionic product must exceed \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}\). To prevent precipitation, the ionic product must be less than or equal to \(K_{\mathrm{sp}}\). At the point of preventing precipitation, we consider the equilibrium condition:
$$
[Zn^{2+}][S^{2-}] = K_{\mathrm{sp}}
$$
Given \([Zn^{2+}] = 0.05\) M and \(K_{\mathrm{sp}} (ZnS) = 1.25 \times 10^{-22}\).
$$
[S^{2-}] = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{-22}}{0.05}
$$
$$
[S^{2-}] = 2.5 \times 10^{-21}\ \mathrm{M}
$$

### Step 2: Use the overall dissociation constant of \(H_{2}S\) to find the required \(H^{+}\) concentration.

The overall dissociation of \(H_{2}S\) is given by:
H_{2}S \rightleftharpoons 2H^{+} + S^{2-}
The overall dissociation constant \(K_{\mathrm{NET}}\) is given as \(1 \times 10^{-21}\).
$$
K_{\mathrm{NET}} = \frac{[H^{+}]^{2}[S^{2-}]}{[H_{2}S]}
$$
Given \([H_{2}S] = 0.1\) M (saturated solution) and we calculated \([S^{2-}] = 2.5 \times 10^{-21}\) M.
$$
1 \times 10^{-21} = \frac{[H^{+}]^{2} \times 2.5 \times 10^{-21}}{0.1}
$$
$$
[H^{+}]^{2} = \frac{1 \times 10^{-21} \times 0.1}{2.5 \times 10^{-21}}
$$
$$
[H^{+}]^{2} = \frac{0.1}{2.5}
$$
$$
[H^{+}]^{2} = \frac{1}{25}
$$
$$
[H^{+}] = \sqrt{\frac{1}{25}}
$$
$$
[H^{+}] = \frac{1}{5}\ \mathrm{M} = 0.2\ \mathrm{M}
$$
Thus, the minimum molar concentration of \(H^{+}\) required to prevent the precipitation of \(ZnS\) is \(0.2\) M.

[Given : $pK_{a1}$ and $pK_{a2}$ of $H_{2}CO_{3}$ are 6.37 and 10.32, respectively ; $\log 2 = 0.30$]

This forms a buffer system with \(NaHCO_{3}\) (acid) and \(Na_{2}CO_{3}\) (salt).

questions.question: Concentration of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ and $Na_{2}SO_{4}$ in a solution is 1 M and $1.8 \times 10^{-2}$ M, respectively. Molar solubility of $PbSO_{4}$ in the same solution is $X \times 10^{-Y}$ M (expressed in scientific notation). The value of Y is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$ . [Given: Solubility product of $PbSO_{4}$ ($K_{sp}$) = $1.6 \times 10^{-8}$. For $H_{2}SO_{4}$, $K_{a1}$ is very large and $K_{a2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}$]
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Dissociation of \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) and \(Na_{2}SO_{4}\)

H_{2}SO_{4} \rightleftharpoons HSO_{4}^{-} + H^{+}
Initial: 1M \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) dissociates completely (since \(K_{a1}\) is very large) to give 1M \(HSO_{4}^{-}\) and 1M \(H^{+}\).
Na_{2}SO_{4} \longrightarrow 2Na^{+} + SO_{4}^{2-}
Initial: \(1.8 \times 10^{-2}\) M \(Na_{2}SO_{4}\) dissociates completely to give \(1.8 \times 10^{-2}\) M \(SO_{4}^{2-}\).

### Step 2: Equilibrium for \(HSO_{4}^{-}\) dissociation

$$
HSO_{4}^{-} \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + SO_{4}^{2-}; K_{a2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2} M
$$
Initial concentrations:
$$
[HSO_{4}^{-}] = 1M
$$
$$
[H^{+}] = 1M
$$
$$
[SO_{4}^{2-}] = 1.8 \times 10^{-2} M
$$
Calculate reaction quotient \(Q_{c}\):
$$
Q_{c} = \frac{[H^{+}][SO_{4}^{2-}]}{[HSO_{4}^{-}]} = \frac{(1)(1.8 \times 10^{-2})}{1} = 1.8 \times 10^{-2}
$$
Since \(Q_{c} (1.8 \times 10^{-2}) > K_{a2} (1.2 \times 10^{-2})\), the reaction will move in backward direction.
Let \(x\) be the change in concentration:
Initial | 1M | 1M | \(1.8 \times 10^{-2}\) M
Change | +x | -x | -x
Equilibrium | \(1+x\) | \(1-x\) | \(1.8 \times 10^{-2} - x\)
$$
K_{a2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2} = \frac{(1-x)(1.8 \times 10^{-2} - x)}{(1+x)}
$$
Since \(x\) is very small, we can approximate \((1+x) \approx 1\) and \((1-x) \approx 1\).
$$
1.2 \times 10^{-2} = \frac{(1)(1.8 \times 10^{-2} - x)}{(1)}
$$
$$
1.2 \times 10^{-2} = 1.8 \times 10^{-2} - x
$$
$$
x = 1.8 \times 10^{-2} - 1.2 \times 10^{-2} = 0.6 \times 10^{-2} M
$$
$$
[SO_{4}^{2-}] = 1.8 \times 10^{-2} - x = 1.8 \times 10^{-2} - 0.6 \times 10^{-2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2} M
$$

### Step 3: Solubility of \(PbSO_{4}\)

PbSO_{4}(s) \rightleftharpoons Pb^{2+}(aq) + SO_{4}^{2-}(aq)
Let \(s\) be the molar solubility of \(PbSO_{4}\).
Initial | s | - | \(1.2 \times 10^{-2}\) M
Equilibrium | - | s | \(s + 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\)
$$
K_{sp} = [Pb^{2+}][SO_{4}^{2-}] = s(s + 1.2 \times 10^{-2}) = 1.6 \times 10^{-8}
$$
Since \(s\) is very small compared to \(1.2 \times 10^{-2}\), we can approximate \((s + 1.2 \times 10^{-2}) \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\).
$$
s(1.2 \times 10^{-2}) = 1.6 \times 10^{-8}
$$
$$
s = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-8}}{1.2 \times 10^{-2}} = \frac{1.6}{1.2} \times 10^{-6} M
$$
$$
s = \frac{4}{3} \times 10^{-6} M \approx 1.33 \times 10^{-6} M
$$
The molar solubility is given as \(X \times 10^{-Y}\) M.
$$
Comparing \(s = 1.33 \times 10^{-6}\) M with \(X \times 10^{-Y}\) M, we get \(Y = 6\).
$$

questions.question: On decreasing the pH from 7 to 2, the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt (MX) of a weak acid (HX) increased from $10^{-4}$ mol $L^{-1}$ to $10^{-3}$ mol $L^{-1}$. The $pK_{a}$ of HX is:
questions.explanation:
$$
At \(pH = 7 \Rightarrow\) pure water
$$
$$
solubility = \(S_{1} = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\)
$$
$$
At \(pH = 2\)
$$
MX(s) + aq \xrightleftharpoons[K_{sp}]{} M^{+}(aq) + X^{-}(aq)
X^{-}(aq) + H^{+}(aq) \xrightleftharpoons[1/K_{a}]{} HX(aq)
Initial concentrations:
$$
\begin{array}{cccc} & X^{-}(aq) & + H^{+}(aq) & \rightleftharpoons HX(aq) \\ \text{Initial} & s & 10^{-2} & 0 \\ \text{Equil.} & s-x & 10^{-2} & x \end{array}
$$
Approximation : \(s - x \approx 0\) [\(X^{-}\) is limiting reagent]
\(\Rightarrow s \approx x\)
$$
s(s - x) = K_{sp} \quad \dots (1)
$$
$$
\frac{s}{(s - x) (10^{-2})} = \frac{1}{K_{a}} \quad \dots (2)
$$
$$
Multiply (1) \(\times\) (2) \(\Rightarrow \frac{s^{2}}{10^{-2}} = \frac{K_{sp}}{K_{a}}\)
$$
$$
\Rightarrow s = \frac{\sqrt{K_{sp}}}{10\sqrt{K_{a}}}
$$
$$
Now given : \(\frac{s}{s_{1}} = \frac{10^{-3}}{10^{-4}}\)
$$
$$
\Rightarrow \frac{\frac{\sqrt{K_{sp}}}{10\sqrt{K_{a}}}}{\sqrt{K_{sp}}} = 10
$$
$$
\Rightarrow \frac{1}{10\sqrt{K_{a}}} = 10
$$
$$
\Rightarrow \sqrt{K_{a}} = 10^{-2}
$$
$$
\Rightarrow K_{a} = 10^{-4}
$$
$$
\Rightarrow pK_{a} = 4
$$

questions.question: For the following reaction, the equilibrium constant $K_{c}$ at 298 K is $1.6 \times 10^{17}$. $Fe^{2+}_{ (aq)} + S^{2-}_{ (aq)} \rightleftharpoons$ FeS(s) When equal volumes of 0.06 M $Fe^{2+}_{ (aq)}$ and 0.2 M $S^{2-}_{ (aq)}$ solutions are mixed, the equilibrium concentration of $Fe^{2+}_{ (aq)}$ is found to be $Y \times 10^{-17}$ M. The value of Y is $ \_ \_ \_ \_ \_ $.
questions.explanation:
The given reaction is:
Fe^{2+}_{ (aq.)} + S^{2-}_{ (aq.)} \rightleftharpoons FeS(s)
When equal volumes of 0.06 M \(Fe^{2+}_{ (aq)}\) and 0.2 M \(S^{2-}_{ (aq)}\) solutions are mixed, the initial concentrations become half:
$$
\begin{array}{ccc} \text{Initial} & 0.03 \text{ M} & 0.1 \text{ M} \\ \text{Equilibrium} & (0.03-x) & (0.1-x) \end{array}
$$
Since the equilibrium constant \(K_{c}\) is very large (\(1.6 \times 10^{17}\)), the reaction proceeds almost to completion. The limiting reactant \(Fe^{2+}_{ (aq.)}\) will be almost entirely consumed.
$$
K_{c} \gg 10^{3} \Rightarrow 0.03-x \approx 0 \Rightarrow x = 0.03
$$
$$
At equilibrium, the concentration of \(Fe^{2+}_{ (aq.)}\) is \(y\) and \(S^{2-}_{ (aq.)}\) is \(0.1 - x = 0.1 - 0.03 = 0.07\) M.
$$
$$
\begin{array}{ccc} \text{Equilibrium} & \approx y & \approx 0.07 \end{array}
$$
The equilibrium constant expression for the reaction is:
$$
K_{c} = \frac{1}{[Fe^{2+}_{ (aq.)}][S^{2-}_{ (aq.)}]}
$$
Substituting the equilibrium concentrations and \(K_{c}\) value:
$$
1.6 \times 10^{17} = \frac{1}{y \times 0.07}
$$
Solving for \(y\):
$$
y = \frac{1}{1.6 \times 10^{17} \times 0.07} = \frac{10^{-17}}{1.6 \times 0.07}
$$
$$
y = \frac{10^{-17}}{0.112} = 8.928 \times 10^{-17}
$$
The equilibrium concentration of \(Fe^{2+}_{ (aq)}\) is given as \(Y \times 10^{-17}\) M. Comparing this with the calculated value of \(y\):
$$
Y \times 10^{-17} = 8.928 \times 10^{-17}
$$
$$
Y = 8.928 \approx 8.93
$$
